column1: What three invariant problems must every theory of political legitimacy solve simultaneously?
column2: 1) The problem of obligation (why citizens should constrain self-interest), 2) the problem of justification (why authority is morally justified, not merely effective), 3) the problem of limits (what boundaries constrain legitimate state action).

column1: Why does a theory that justifies authority without establishing limits risk totalitarianism, according to the legitimacy framework?
column2: Because without limits, any exercise of power can be retroactively justified as legitimate, removing the conceptual check that distinguishes rightful authority from unconstrained domination.

column1: What is Rawls's 'original position' and what mechanism makes it function?
column2: A hypothetical contracting scenario in which rational agents choose principles of justice behind a 'veil of ignorance' that conceals their talents, class, race, gender, and conception of the good—forcing impartial choice since no one knows their eventual social position.

column1: State Rawls's two principles of justice.
column2: 1) Each person has an equal claim to a fully adequate scheme of basic liberties compatible with the same scheme for all. 2) Social/economic inequalities must be attached to offices open under fair equality of opportunity, and must benefit the least advantaged (the difference principle).

column1: What decision rule does Rawls use to justify the difference principle, and what does it imply?
column2: The maximin rule: behind the veil of ignorance, rational agents maximize the minimum possible outcome since they cannot assign probabilities to their future social position—this justifies prioritizing the worst-off.

column1: How does Nozick's entitlement theory of justice differ fundamentally from Rawls's framework?
column2: Nozick rejects patterned/end-state distributive justice entirely, arguing justice concerns the historical entitlement of holdings (just acquisition and just transfer) rather than any target distribution pattern.

column1: Define Isaiah Berlin's distinction between negative and positive liberty.
column2: Negative liberty = freedom FROM external interference (absence of obstacles to action). Positive liberty = freedom TO achieve self-mastery and rational self-direction (autonomy and genuine self-governance).

column1: Common misconception: Does extensive negative liberty guarantee positive liberty? Give the canonical counterexample.
column2: No. An addict facing no legal prohibition on drug use has extensive negative liberty but lacks positive liberty, since their choices reflect compulsion rather than genuine self-governance.

column1: What is the foundational tension that all democratic theory must navigate?
column2: The people cannot all participate in every decision simultaneously, yet democratic legitimacy requires that political power ultimately derive from the governed—creating the problem of converting heterogeneous preferences into binding collective decisions.

column1: How does Rousseau's 'general will' differ from classical liberal consent theory (Hobbes/Locke) regarding democratic legitimacy?
column2: Liberal consent theory grounds legitimacy in individuals consenting to a constitutional framework (majority rule legitimate because minorities also consented to the rules). Rousseau's general will claims a collective wisdom transcending mere aggregation of individual preferences.

column1: What is the core shared diagnosis of communitarian/recognition-theory critiques (MacIntyre, Sandel, Honneth, Kymlicka) against liberal neutrality?
column2: Liberal neutrality is neither truly neutral nor universally just—it conceals particular cultural assumptions (e.g., Enlightenment individualism/secularity) and systematically disadvantages identities falling outside that implicit norm, achieving invisibility rather than neutrality.

column1: What are the three intertwined puzzles of global justice identified in the cosmopolitan debate?
column2: 1) The jurisdictional puzzle (why borders should determine moral responsibility), 2) the institutional puzzle (whether distributive justice requires shared coercive institutions, per Rawls's Law of Peoples), 3) the commitment puzzle (what binds individuals/states to strangers across borders absent reciprocity).
